meta.title: Agent Safety and Sandboxing
meta.thesis: Agent Safety and Sandboxing is practical when learners can apply it to this concrete case: A browser agent can read invoices but must not send emails or download files without approval. By the end, they should be able to build or review sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent, measure blocked unsafe action count, and catch the failure where a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect.

blocks.title: Why Agent Safety and Sandboxing matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A browser agent can read invoices but must not send emails or download files without approval. The learner's job is not to memorize Agent Safety and Sandboxing; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved blocked unsafe action count.

Running case: sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson skips definition-drilling and spends its effort on edge cases: state boundaries, hidden coupling, observability gaps, and the evidence that would change a production decision.

items.text: Product framing: Agent Safety and Sandboxing matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Agent Safety and Sandboxing matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure blocked unsafe action count on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent

spans.text: Scenario: A browser agent can read invoices but must not send emails or download files without approval. The team wants to improve blocked unsafe action count, but it has already seen this failure: a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect.
Here is the worked artifact at design-review depth: concrete enough to inspect, small enough to build as a thin slice.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Launch review: a customer-facing AI feature touches user data, external tools, or regulated decisions. The team needs a risk classification and controls before it ships.

Artifact: sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent. It maps data flows, user harms, threat scenarios, required controls, human review, logging, and the release evidence for blocked unsafe action count.
Worked output: classify the feature, identify sensitive data, block unsafe tool use, add audit logging, test a misuse case, and assign an owner for unresolved risk.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: AI safety reviewer. Context: A browser agent can read invoices but must not send emails or download files without approval. Task: complete a risk review for sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent. Include data handled, user harm, tool risk, misuse test, mitigation, owner, and release decision. Output: {risk_category, controls, tests, unresolved_risks, owner}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Agent Safety and Sandboxing to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: blocked unsafe action count becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Agent Safety and Sandboxing design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

The wrong move is to jump straight to the fanciest option. The useful move is to ask which option improves blocked unsafe action count while making this failure visible: a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: A policy exists in prose but is not enforced at the tool, data, or release boundary.
The system passes benign tests but follows instructions embedded in untrusted content.
Sensitive data is minimized in the app but retained in logs or traces.
The broad warning sign: blocked unsafe action count gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect.

For sandbox permission table for a tool-using operations agent, the sketch should prove one thing: the system can improve blocked unsafe action count without hiding the failure where a harmless-looking web step triggers an irreversible side effect.
